passages.text: Today the World Health Organization launched a comprehensive Repository of systematic reviews on interventions in environment, climate change and health . The Repository aims to assess the current state of evidence and to provide a list of systematic reviews on interventions in all major areas of environment, climate change and health (ECH). Areas of ECH covered by the Repository have been defined based on the Compendium of WHO and other UN guidance on health and environment and include air quality, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), climate change, solid waste, chemicals, radiation, nature and health, safe environments and mobility, safe and healthy food, environmental noise, and priority settings for action. Examples of systematic reviews that were considered for inclusion in the Repository include those examining various types of intervention, such as policies, practices, and educational interventions, with the aim to improve health outcomes or reduce harmful exposures.

“Implementing effective environmental health interventions can save millions of lives every year,” said Dr Maria Neira, Director, Department of Environment, Climate Change and Health, World Health Organization. “Policy-makers need to be informed on how to withstand environmental shocks and protect populations. This Repository presents the existing knowledge on the most effective interventions that can be implemented and will help policy-makers to make the right decision.”

In an era marked by escalating environmental challenges and their profound implications on public health, the launch of this Repository marks a milestone in WHO's ongoing efforts to safeguard global health and well-being. This Repository serves as a catalyst and spotlights existing knowledge and evidence on the most effective interventions to be taken. By highlighting these measures, WHO can assist decision-makers and practitioners at national, regional and municipal levels in identifying and implementing most effective environmental health policies. This Repository may also be used to point out current knowledge gaps and stimulate research in areas in which evidence is needed.

Deciding if and where to use rapid methods in qualitative research Rapid reviews are a type of literature review product that is adapted from a systematic review by using an accelerated and more streamlined methodology. This training package includes guidance on how to conduct rapid reviews in practice with supplementary materials for optional reading. At the end, there is also a small collection of databases for reference.
Key learning objectives include:
differentiating rapid reviews from systematic reviews and other evidence synthesis methodologies;
understanding the steps involved in undertaking a rapid review;
describing how rapid reviews can vary in scope and methodology.

The text resource below is a step by step guide with an accompanying webinar on the process of conducting a rapid review. The webinar resource presents insights from the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute (OHRI) on their experiences conducting rapid reviews and a discussion on the challenges, opportunities and lessons learned.

Rapid reviews are a type of knowledge synthesis in which

develop, and implement health policies.

evidence products
Description
Inventories

Inventories only list the evidence that is available on a given topic. There
is no attempt to appraise, summarize or synthesize the evidence for
further use, nor is there an attempt to present conclusions or
recommendations to the knowledge user.

Rapid response
briefs

Rapid response briefs present a summary of the best available evidence
in a synthesized and contextualized manner, in direct response to a
decision-maker’s question. They are knowledge translation products
created through formal methods to synthesize and appraise the
evidence. They do not generate new knowledge, but use findings that
are already available, especially from existing systematic reviews.
Rapid reviews

Rapid reviews represent a knowledge generation strategy. They
synthesize findings and assess the validity of research evidence using
“abbreviated” systematic review methods, modifying these methods to
generate evidence in a short time.

passages.text: Answer: Joints (knuckles) are covered by a capsule (the joint capsule or synovial capsule). Within the space of this capsule the synovial fluid is contained which acts as a lubricant and also contains nutrients for the adjacent bone surfaces. A variety of gases are continuously dissolved in this fluid. When one cracks a knuckle, the stretching of the capsule lowers the pressure inside the joint and creates a vacuum which is filled by the gas previously dissolved in the synovial fluid. This creates a “bubble” which then bursts producing the characteristic “popping” or “cracking” sound. It takes a while until these gases are re-dissolved in the synovial fluid which explains why knuckles cannot be “re-cracked” immediately.

A study found that after many years of cracking habitual knuckle crackers may have reduced grip strength compared with people not cracking their knuckles.

passages.text: People often ask me, "Am I going to get arthritis because I crack my knuckles?" This topic is controversial even among medical professionals. 1 Yildizgören MT, Ekiz T, Nizamogullari S, Turhanoglu AD, Guler H, Ustun N, Kara M, Özçakar L. Effects of habitual knuckle cracking on metacarpal cartilage thickness and grip strength . Hand Surg Rehabil. 2017 Feb;36(1):41-43. doi: 10.1016/j.hansur.2016.09.001. Epub 2016 Oct 11. PubMed PMID: 28137441 Research gives us some insights.
Located where the fingers meet the hand, knuckles are sometimes called metacarpophalangeal joints (MCPs).
The clicking, cracking, popping, or snapping that occurs when you crack your knuckles is associated with tiny gas bubbles.

To produce a cracking sensation, a finger is forced forward or backward (doctors call this hyper-flexion or hyper-extension at a metacarpophalangeal joint) or pulled straight away from the hand. Any of these movements can cause a change in pressure in the joint. The pressure change causes tiny gas bubbles to form in the knuckle’s joint fluid.

It is not clear whether the cracking noise is produced when bubbles form or when the bubbles pop. 2 Rizvi A, Loukas M, Oskouian RJ, Tubbs RS. Let's get a hand on this: Review of the clinical anatomy of "knuckle cracking" . Clin Anat. 2018 Sep;31(6):942-945. doi: 10.1002/ca.23243. Epub 2018 Oct 18. Review. PubMed PMID: 30080300.

It usually takes 15 or 20 minutes for the gas bubbles to dissipate and for the bones of the joint to return to their normal positions. 3 Unsworth A, Dowson D, Wright V. 1971. ̳Cracking joints‘ A bioengineering study of cavitation in the metacarpophalangeal joint. Ann Rheum Dis 30:348–358. As cited in Rizvi 2018. This is why you can’t crack the same knuckle twice in a row.
It seems logical that habitual knuckle cracking causes arthritis or other degenerative changes in the hand. But what do medical researchers say?

Research studies comparing knuckle crackers' to non-crackers have had mixed results. 1 Yildizgören MT, Ekiz T, Nizamogullari S, Turhanoglu AD, Guler H, Ustun N, Kara M, Özçakar L. Effects of habitual knuckle cracking on metacarpal cartilage thickness and grip strength . Hand Surg Rehabil. 2017 Feb;36(1):41-43. doi: 10.1016/j.hansur.2016.09.001. Epub 2016 Oct 11. PubMed PMID: 28137441 A couple of studies have reported an association between knuckle cracking and hand arthritis. 4 Watson P, Hamilton A, Mollan R. Habitual joint cracking and radiological damage. BMJ 1989;299:1566. , 5 Watson P, Kernohan WG, Mollan RA. A study of the cracking sounds from the metacarpophalangeal joint. Proc Inst Mech Eng 1989;203:109–18. Others found no significant connection. 6 Deweber K, Olszewski M, Ortolano R. Knuckle cracking and hand osteoarthritis. J Am Board Fam Med 2011;24:169–74. , 7 Castellanos J, Axelrod D. Effect of habitual knuckle cracking on hand function. Ann Rheum Dis. 1990;49(5):308–309. doi:10.1136/ard.49.5.308

passages.text: Executive summary
passages.heading_path: Cracking your knuckles causes osteoarthritis and other bone diseases.

passages.text: Decades of clinical research and reviews find no convincing evidence that habitual knuckle cracking causes osteoarthritis: large observational studies report similar rates of hand OA among crackers and non-crackers (e.g., 18.1% vs. 21.5%) and multiple expert summaries conclude no causal link [1] [2] [3] . However, some studies report associations with hand swelling , reduced grip strength , and theoretical mechanical concerns from in‑vitro force measurements, so the practice is not entirely free of possible minor harms [4] [5] [2] .
passages.heading_path: Cracking your knuckles causes osteoarthritis and other bone diseases.

passages.text: 1. The direct question — does knuckle cracking cause osteoarthritis?
passages.heading_path: Cracking your knuckles causes osteoarthritis and other bone diseases.

passages.text: The best available clinical data do not support the claim that cracking knuckles leads to osteoarthritis: a retrospective case‑control study that compared radiographs in people aged 50–89 found no increased prevalence of hand OA among habitual knuckle crackers and concluded cracking is not a risk factor for hand OA [1] [6] [2] . Multiple health organizations and summaries echo that conclusion—reviews and patient‑facing resources state there is no known correlation between knuckle cracking and arthritis [3] [7] [8] .
passages.heading_path: Cracking your knuckles causes osteoarthritis and other bone diseases.

passages.text: 2. Where the worry comes from — plausible mechanics and lab findings
passages.heading_path: Cracking your knuckles causes osteoarthritis and other bone diseases.

passages.text: Skepticism about knuckle‑cracking’s safety arises from plausible mechanical mechanisms: cavitation (gas bubble formation and collapse) in the joint produces audible pops, and in vitro experiments show the forces involved can exceed thresholds that, in theory, might damage articular cartilage; analogies to propeller cavitation are invoked to explain possible surface wear [2] . Those biomechanical observations create a biologically plausible pathway for harm, but plausibility alone does not establish that habitual cracking produces clinically meaningful cartilage loss or OA in humans, and the clinical literature has not borne out that causal chain [2] .
passages.heading_path: Cracking your knuckles causes osteoarthritis and other bone diseases.

passages.text: 3. Conflicting or concerning findings beyond osteoarthritis
passages.heading_path: Cracking your knuckles causes osteoarthritis and other bone diseases.

passages.text: While osteoarthritis risk appears unchanged, some studies report other associations: a study examining hand function found habitual knuckle cracking correlated with hand swelling and weaker grip strength, and sonography studies document intra‑articular gas following distraction maneuvers [4] [5] . These findings raise the possibility of functional or soft‑tissue effects even if frank OA does not develop, and different studies vary in size and methodology, leaving room for nuance in interpreting clinical significance [4] [5] .
passages.heading_path: Cracking your knuckles causes osteoarthritis and other bone diseases.

passages.text: 4. Limitations of existing research and what remains uncertain
passages.heading_path: Cracking your knuckles causes osteoarthritis and other bone diseases.

passages.text: Most evidence comes from observational and retrospective studies with modest sample sizes and varied outcome measures, so they can show lack of association but are limited in proving absolute safety over decades and in all subpopulations; longitudinal, large‑scale prospective trials are scarce [6] [2] . The mechanistic lab data suggest a theoretical risk but do not equate to demonstrated long‑term joint damage in real‑world habitual crackers, and some small studies hint at functional differences that merit further study rather than definitive conclusions [2] [4] .
passages.heading_path: Cracking your knuckles causes osteoarthritis and other bone diseases.

passages.text: 5. Practical takeaways — balance of evidence and reasonable precautions
passages.heading_path: Cracking your knuckles causes osteoarthritis and other bone diseases.

passages.text: The balance of evidence from clinical studies and expert summaries is clear: habitual knuckle cracking has not been shown to increase the risk of osteoarthritis [1] [2] [3] . Still, given reports of swelling, weaker grip in some cohorts, and rare case reports of acute ligamentous injury with aggressive manipulation, those who experience pain, persistent swelling, or functional decline should avoid the habit and seek evaluation; for the general population, the noise and social annoyance remain the main downsides more than demonstrable OA risk [4] [5] [9] .
